column2: Here, twice-born, one should first make the salutation in the "svastika" posture, taking the bow in the left hand and the arrow in the right.
In the Vaishakha stance, whether standing or extended, having set the string on the bow, the lover of the bow —
having set the lower middle of the bow and the point of the arrow on the ground and having weighed it likewise,
with the arms, elbows and forearms, of good vow: he whose arrow and bow are best, and at the notch of the arrow,
the placing and the bow have twelve fingers' interval; it should be made distinguished by the string, not too little nor too much.
Having placed the bow at the navel and the bundle of arrows on the hip, one should raise the lifted hand between eye and ear;
the arrow on the right at the breast-tip should be held by the former fist; then having taken it, one should quickly extend it forward;
not inside, nor outside, not up, nor down, not bent, not supine, not moving, not too wrapped,
even, endowed with steadiness, standing like the former staff; then, having covered the target with this former fist,
the archer risen with chest, standing bent in a triangle, with loosened shoulder and unmoving neck, head peacock-curved,
forehead, nose, mouth and shoulders should make it horse-like. The interval between chin and shoulder is to be known as three fingers;
the first is to be known as three fingers, the second two fingers, the third is declared one finger — the stretch between chin and shoulders.
Having taken the arrow by the feather end with forefinger and thumb, then again with ring finger and likewise the middle,
one should draw with speed until the arrow is well filled; having thus begun, the bird (arrow) should be released by rule.
The one of good vow should pierce with the arrow the target struck by gaze and fist; having released, the rear hand should be flung quickly behind.
They desire this as the uprooting; it should be known by you, twice-born. The elbow should be set below by the archer who has drawn;
in release it should be done upward; in joining the target it is middle; the best, the foremost, is to be known by those expert in archery.
The best arrow is to be known as of twelve fists; likewise eleven; the least of ten fists.
A bow of four cubits is best; three and a half middling; of three cubits is declared the least, always for infantry;
for horse, chariot and the best elephant the same is declared.
Having fixed the mind on the target with the fist, the knower of rule, on the right part of the body, should release the arrow, coloring it.
One should place the staff on the target in the position of the forehead-hollow; having drawn it, he should strike there the "chandraka" of sixteen fingers;
then, having released the arrow, one trained in the "ulka" should hold repeatedly with the middle finger,
should shoot the eye-target from the quiver and the right four-sided; one should practice piercing the four-sided one, standing from the beginning;
after that the sharp, the turned and the gone, the low and the high piercing; then one should practice quick shooting.
In these piercing-places from the pouch of the quarry, one should threaten with the bow by hundreds of varied, hard-to-cross hand-motions.
Among them, Brahmin, two targets are called firm, two hard, two hard-to-pierce and two variegated-hard;
low and sharp are not declared in the firm target; the low is declared hard, and the one going upward;
in the middle of the head-path are the variegated-hard ones. Having made the group of targets thus, with right and with the other,
the hero should first ascend, then the man who has conquered the mark. This same rule is stated, seen there by practitioners;
its greater turning is declared from that target. He should fix the target there, firm in the arrow's feather;
it may be turning, moving or steady; from all sides he should strike, pierce, cut and pain.
The knower of the rule of yoga in action, having so known, should perform the rule. By mind, eye and sight the yoga-learner conquers Yama.
Having made a ring shape, a whirling thing above the head, he should quickly throw at a quickly-made man wrapped in hide;
in leaping and jumping and likewise against renunciants, having made the rule of equal yoga, one should apply the well-trained.
Having conquered according to rule, then he should perform binding: having bound the sword at the waist, hanging on the left side,
having held it firmly with the left he should draw it with the right. Six fingers in girth, seven cubits high,
iron rods and varied armors; in half a cubit, equal, oblique and upward —
hear, by what rule one should apply it, from Angada: having placed a new firm one with limbs covered by quiver-hide,
taking in the hand a new club, with right fingers, raising it one should strike; by that the destruction of the child (target) is sure;
with both hands then one should make its fall; doing it without trouble, success in killing is declared.
For the exercise of vehicles, long ago for movement, for you.
Uddhuta and avadhuta, left and right, analakshita and visphota, karala, indra and mahasakha,
vikaralanipata, vibhishana and bhayanaka, samagra, ardha, tritiyamsha, pada, padardha, varija,
pratyalidha, alidha, varaha and lulita — thus thirty-two are to be known in sword and shield rules in battle.
Paravritta, apavritta, grihita, laghu-named, urdhvakshipta, adhahkshipta, sandharita, vidharita,
shyenapata, gajapata, and graha-grahya likewise — thus eleven kinds are to be known of the noose-types of men.
Rijvayata, vishala, and tiryagbhramita — five actions are declared by the great for the scattered noose.
Cutting, piercing, falling, whirling, lying, splitting, severing and this wheel work;
asphota, kshedana, bheda, trasa and andolitaka — know these as spear actions; the sixth is called aghata.
Eye-blow, arm-blow, side-blow, best of twice-born; the fall by straight-winged arrow is declared of the javelin (tomara);
ahata, Brahmin, gomutra, prabhutanka, kamalasana; then urdhvagatra, namita, left and right,
avritta and paravritta, padoddhuta, aplvuta, hamsamarda and vimarda — mace work is declared.
Karala, avaghata and dashopaplutaka, kshiptahasta, sthita, shunya — one should declare for the parashu (axe).
Striking, cutting, Brahmin, and crushing, likewise leaping and killing — these are the actions of the mudgara (mallet);
sanshranta, vishranta, govisarga, sudurdhara — these are the actions of the bhindipala and of the club.
Antya, madhya, paravritta, nideshanta, best of twice-born — these are the actions of the vajra and of the pattisha.
Seizing, cutting, striking, lifting the force, extension — the work of the sword (kripana) is declared; felling and bursting likewise;
frightening, guarding, striking, lifting the force, extension — the work of the kshepani is declared; this is also the work of machines.
Santyaga, avadamsha, varahoddhutaka, hastavahasta, alina, ekahasta, tavahasta,
dvihasta, bahupasha, katirechitaka, udgata, chest-and-forehead blow, and bhujavidhamana;
karoddhuta, vimana, padahati, vipadika, gatrasamshleshana, shanta, and gatraviparyaya,
urdhvaprahara and ghata, gomutra, savya and dakshina, parantaraka, danda, karaviradha, akula,
tiryagbandha, apamarga, bhimavega, sudarshana, simhakranta, gajakranta and gardabhakranta —
know these as mace actions, and now the action of wrestling: drawing, drawing away, the roots of the arms,
neck-turning, the terrible back-breaking, paryasana and viparyasa, pashumara, ajavika,
foot-blow, asphota, and katirechitaka, body-embrace, skandhagata, mahivyajana,
chest-and-forehead blow, and vispashtakarana; uddhuta and avadhuta, tiryanmargagata,
gajaskandha, avakshepa, aparangmukha, devamarga, adhomarga, and amargagamanakula,
yashtighata, avakshepa, vasudhadarana, janubandha, bhujabandha, the very terrible,
viprishtha, sodaka, shubhra and bhujaveshtita. Armed men must be ready in battle with weapons, on elephants and the rest.
Two with excellent goads, one at the neck, another; two at the shoulders, two bowmen and two sword-bearers on an elephant;
for chariots, for battle, for elephants and horses there should be three; three bowmen are said for the protection of a horse,
one should appoint a shield-bearer for the protection of the archers. Having worshipped the weapon with one's own mantras, the science that bewilders the three worlds,
he who goes to battle conquers enemies and protects the earth.
